history.title: Find Your Way

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

A map is not a photograph. Somebody decided what to draw and what to leave out. This week you learn to read a map, and to notice the choices behind it.

1. Read **Every Map Leaves Something Out**.
2. Learn the words in **Map Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Memory** game.
3. Keep the **Parts of a Map** chart where you can see it.
4. Sort the cards in **On the Map or Not?**
5. Practise explaining with **Map Frames**, then check yourself against the rubric.
6. Take **Map Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Map Parts**.
8. Read **Map Questions Kids Ask** when you get curious.
9. Finish with **Design: A Map of Somewhere You Know**.

Your job this week: find a real map somewhere — a bus stop, a mall, a park sign — and see which parts it has. 🗺️

history.title: Every Map Leaves Something Out
history.data:
## Every Map Leaves Something Out

Draw a map of your classroom. Did you draw every pencil? Every crumb on the floor? Of course not. You drew the desks and the door.

That is the first thing to know about maps. A **map** is a drawing of a place from above, and it always leaves things out on purpose. A map that showed everything would be as big and as confusing as the real place.

So a mapmaker chooses. And once you know that, you can ask a much better question than "where is it?" You can ask: what did this person decide to show me?

Maps give you tools for reading them.

A **symbol** is a small picture that stands for something real. A tiny tent means a campground. A blue line means a river. The **key** is the box that tells you what each symbol means. Without a key, a symbol is just a shape.

The **compass** rose shows you which way is north. Most maps put north at the top, but that is a habit, not a rule. Old maps often put east at the top instead.

The **scale** tells you how much real distance a small distance on the paper stands for. One inch might mean one mile. Scale is why a whole country can sit on one page.

A **border** is a line showing where one place ends and the next begins. Some borders follow a river. Many were drawn by people, and people argued about them.

A **globe** is different from a flat map. Earth is round, so flattening it always stretches something. On many flat maps Greenland looks about the size of Africa. It is not close. Africa is about fourteen times larger.

So read a map twice. Once to find your way. Once to ask what got left out.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Map Reader |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading the parts | Points at the map | Uses the key or compass correctly | Uses key, compass and scale together to answer a question |
| Map words | Everyday words only | Uses 1-2 glossary words correctly | Uses 3+ glossary words correctly, including symbol and key |

history.title: Map Check

questions.question: You see a small tent drawn on a map. Where do you find out what it means?
options: In the key, which explains every symbol
In the scale, which measures the distance
On the compass, which points you north
Along the border, which marks the edges
questions.correctAnswer: In the key, which explains every symbol

questions.question: Why does a map leave things out?
options: The mapmaker ran out of room on the paper
Showing everything would be as confusing as the real place
Some things are secret and are not allowed on maps
Only the newest maps have room for all of it
questions.correctAnswer: Showing everything would be as confusing as the real place

questions.question: Is north always at the top of a map?
options: Yes, it is a rule that mapmakers must follow
Yes, because north is the top of the planet
No, it is a habit; old maps often put east up
No, the top changes depending on the season
questions.correctAnswer: No, it is a habit; old maps often put east up
questions.conceptLabel: north on top is a habit

questions.question: On many flat maps Greenland looks about as big as Africa. Why?
options: Greenland really is about that size in real life
The mapmaker measured the ice instead of the land
Africa shrank when countries redrew their borders
Flattening a round Earth stretches some places
questions.correctAnswer: Flattening a round Earth stretches some places
questions.conceptLabel: flat maps stretch the round earth

questions.question: What does the scale on a map tell you?
options: How heavy the paper the map is printed on is
How old the map is and when it was drawn
Which places on the map are the most important
What a small distance on paper means in real life
questions.correctAnswer: What a small distance on paper means in real life
questions.conceptLabel: scale turns paper into real distance

questions.question: Name two things a map of your school would leave out, and say why leaving them out helps.
questions.expectedAnswer: Answers vary. A full answer names two real things that are true but unhelpful, such as where each backpack is or what is for lunch, and explains that leaving them out keeps the map clear enough to use.

questions.question: A friend says a map is just a photo of a place from above. What would you tell them?
questions.expectedAnswer: A map is not a photo. Somebody chose what to draw and what to leave out, and used symbols instead of the real things. A photo would show every car and every crumb, which would make it hard to use.

reflections.text: What is a landmark near your home that you would put on a map?
If you drew a map of your day, what would you leave out?

history.title: Map Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Who decides where a border goes? 🗺️
data.answer: People do. Some borders follow a river or a mountain range. Many were drawn in a room far away, and people have argued about them ever since.

data.question: Why is north at the top? ⬆️
data.answer: Habit, mostly. Old European mapmakers settled on it and it stuck. Some old maps put east at the top instead. Space has no up, so no direction is the real top.

data.question: Is a globe better than a flat map?
data.answer: For shape and size, yes. A globe is round like Earth, so nothing gets stretched. But you cannot fold one into a pocket, and you can only see half at a time.

data.question: How do phone maps know where I am? 📱
data.answer: Your phone listens for signals from satellites far above you. It works out how long each signal took to arrive, and from that it finds your spot.

data.question: Can a map be wrong?
data.answer: Yes, and in two ways. It can have mistakes. It can also be drawn to make one place look bigger or more important than it is. Both are worth watching for.

data.question: Are there places left to map?
data.answer: Plenty. Most of the deep ocean floor has never been mapped closely. We have better maps of the surface of Mars than of the bottom of our own sea.

data.title: A Map of Somewhere You Know
data.instructions: Make a map of one real place for one real purpose. Then say what you left out, and why leaving it out made the map better.
data.fitReason: Drawing a map for a stated purpose forces a student to leave things out on purpose, which is the idea the reading is built on and the part a labeling worksheet never reaches.

brief.context: A new student starts next week and does not know the building. Your class is making maps to help. You get one sheet of paper, coloured pencils, and one class period to walk the route.
brief.audience: The new student, who will use your map alone on their first morning
brief.drivingQuestion: What has to be on a map of our school so a new student can find their way alone, and what has to be left off so it stays easy to read?
brief.seedDirection: Decide the job first. A map for finding the bathroom is a different map from a map for the fire drill.
lockedLessonFacts: A map is a drawing of a place from above.
A key tells you what each symbol means.
A compass shows which way is north.
Every map leaves things out on purpose.
openQuestions: What is the one job this map has to do?
Which symbols will you invent, and how will the key explain them?
What did you decide to leave off, and why?
stakeholders: The teacher who hands out the map
Your partner, who tests it by walking it
criteria: The map has a key, and every symbol on the map is in it
The map has a compass showing north
A partner can walk the route using the map without being told
You can name two things you left out, and say why
constraints: Drawn from above, not from the side
brief.deliverable: The finished map, plus two sentences: the job this map does, and the two things you left off on purpose.

parallelExample.context: A student mapped the route from the front door to the cafeteria.
parallelExample.move: He drew only the hallways on that route and greyed the rest of the building out. He invented three symbols, put them in a key, and his partner walked it without asking a question.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Greying out the rest was a choice, not laziness. The map got easier to use because it showed less.

frameChoices: A map for finding one room
